newsitem.title: LATVIA: Economy minister named as new Latvian premier.
newsitem.headline: Economy minister named as new Latvian premier.

text.p: Latvian Economy Minister Guntar Krasts on Monday won the backing of leading political parties and the president to be the new prime minister of the former Soviet republic.

Krasts, an economist with reform credentials, will replace tough-talking former businessman Andris Shkele, forced to resign amid corruption scandals and a loss of confidence by his seven-party rainbow coalition.
A parliamentary vote on confirming Krasts in office looked likely on August 6, politicians said.
"Of all the candidates, he was the best," said Indulis Berzinsh, a leading member of the second-largest party in parliament, Latvia's Way. "He is not a new man, he has already worked in the cabinet."
President Guntis Ulmanis met leading political parties and agreed formally to nominate Krasts as premier.

"I have signed a decree by which...I invite Guntar Krasts to form the new cabinet of ministers," Ulmanis told reporters. "I think that Guntar Krasts has had the privilege as economy minister to acquaint himself with state affairs."
Diplomats in the Baltic state warned he would have to reconcile the views of a coalition of seven parties - Latvian nationalists, centrists and moderate leftists.
Krasts is a member of the third-largest party in parliament, a nationalist grouping called For Fatherland and Freedom.
The acerbic Shkele, who announced his resignation last week after a year and a half in office, had no political affiliation.
He was credited with advancing the reforms Latvia launched after quitting the former Soviet Union in 1991, but was hit by several ministerial resignations amid corruption scandals.
He had also alienated the seven ruling parties by accusing them of working only in their own interests.
Berzinsh said a parliamentary vote on the appointment could take place on August 6. The coalition has a solid majority of 70 of the 100 seats in the legislature.
Latvia's large Russian-speaking minority -- non-Latvians make up some 45 percent of the population -- has largely been excluded from the political process and most have no vote.
Krasts had been economy minister since Shkele first came to power at the end of 1995.
One local commentator wondered whether he would be able to keep up the pace of reforms set by Shkele.

"One issue is what the new government, which in line-up will very much be the same as the old government, will do with the government declaration," said Askold Rodinsh, a commentator with leading daily Diena, referring to Krasts' legislative programme.
"It (the declaration) provides for reforms at Shkele's pace. Will this government be able to keep this up?" he added.
Shkele came to power in December 1995 as Latvia was trying to recover from a banking crisis caused by the collapse of its largest bank, Banka Baltiya.
His main achievement was to restore order to public finances, bringing the country from a budget deficit of around $180 million to a surplus at the moment of around $60 million.

He also pushed ahead with privatisation, which had stagnated under the previous government, and managed to put Latvia, a candidate for membership of the European Union, more firmly on the international investment map.
